title: I didn't realize Etsy was selling bridges now
summary: The company says its new generative AI training agreement will only be used for good. Why would anyone believe that?
body: Online marketplace Etsy, best known as a platform for selling handmade goods, recently updated its user agreement to allow itself to "develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies" using content uploaded by sellers. This has not gone over well, with some closing their Etsy shops in protest. In response, Etsy has assured users that it doesn't plan to train AI systems designed to copy their work or replace their creativity. Instead, the company said that the change is about improving the platform and providing "services and tools that can help you run your business." I am sometimes sympathetic toward companies that get yelled at for normal terms of service agreements. If a company hosts user-submitted content on the web, for instance, it needs a license to distribute that content globally, and sometimes users misunderstand that. This is not one of those cases. title: 21% of Rockstar staff have been employed by the company for over 10 years, which explains a lot about GTA 6's record-breaking launch
summary: It's easier to make successful games when you hold onto the people who know how.
body: If we're using Metacritic as a metric, Grand Theft Auto 6 is currently the best-reviewed game of all time . Between preorders and launch-day sales, it's already made over $3.7 billion in sales revenue. It's being lauded as a landmark achievement in game design, storytelling, and engineering. So how, exactly, did Rockstar pull it off? Well, the billion-dollar production budget certainly helped. But a Bloomberg report offers an important insight into how GTA 6 was able to deliver on its promises: According to a spokesperson, 21% of Rockstar's staff—roughly 1,000 people—have been employed by the company for over 10 years. For many of its development leads and directors, that figure is closer to 20 years, or higher. (Image credit: Rockstar) By retaining its employees for so long, Rockstar is able to capitalize on the kind of shared, institutional knowledge and honed creative process that developers build through years of collaboration. body: OpenAI has recently reported that its frontier models attempted to rewrite AMD circuits and received an up-to 14% PPA (Power, Performance and Area) boost. OpenAI says these rewrites are "production-viable" too (via BigGo Finance ). The claim is not that humans couldn't make these same optimisations, but instead that it did around a year's worth of design optimisations in less than 5 months, an optimisation of optimisation, if you will. (Okay, I'll stop writing optimisation now.) Apparently, AMD has even incorporated some of these findings into chip designs that have recently gone to manufacturing. The model worked on an in-house "Jalapeño" chip, as well as an AMD "flagship GPU IP" and "AMD next-gen flagship CPU key modules." Each one of these saw different gains. For the Jalapeño vector compute unit, the model's changes managed to reduce cell area by around 13%, and this was observed when powering on the hardware. The Jalapeño compute unit saw the standard cell area reduced by around 10%, with the multiplier area alone reduced by around 15 % and latency cut from two clock cycles to one. title: AMD's next-gen Zen 6 desktop CPUs are rumoured to be delayed, may be pushed back to second half of 2027
summary: A process switch to TSMC N2X is said to be behind the delay.
body: We got our first technical deep dive into AMD's next-generation Zen 6 CPU architecture last week, in the form of the company's new Venice range of server chips. Now there's a rumour that the consumer Ryzen chip launch may have been pushed back to the second half of 2027. The new Ryzen offerings were originally thought to be launching in the first half, but Chiphell leaker Zhang Zhonghao says otherwise. In a post spotted by Videocardz , Zhang Zhonghao claims that the desktop chips, codenamed Olympic Ridge, have been switched to TSMC's N2X manufacturing process, and as a result the "timeline has been pushed back" (via machine translation). Zhang Zhonghao makes mention of Computex in their post, which some are speculating means a launch date after the show in June of next year. Olympic Ridge was originally though to be using TSMC's N2 or N2P process node, but a switch to the performance-focussed N2X would line up with previous rumours that the chips are targeting very high clockspeeds, potentially all the way up to 6.5 GHz . N2X is scheduled to enter production in 2027, which would explain the longer timeframe if this rumour proves out. A delay to the second half of next year would m…

title: PC gamers notice Nvidia's drivers hammering their SSDs with tens of GB/hr of unnecessary writes – revert to 621.01 ASAP
summary: There is a registry fix, but it's surprising to see the driver package still available to download.
body: Another day, another dodgy driver: Nvidia's latest driver package (621.24) is needlessly writing to users' SSDs, in some cases by 30 GB every hour. And if that sounds familiar, it's because an issue with Radeon Adrenalin drivers did a similar thing a week ago. The issue appears to be fairly widespread going from reports on the Nvidia GeForce forum , Dell forum , Super User forum , and many, many threads on Reddit . Though that's a bunch of people that might, and did, notice random writes to their SSD; many more may not visit their task manager to check these things with any regularity. To check your own PC: Open Task Manager Open Details tab Right click on column header Click Select columns Find and select I/O write bytes Look for 'NVDisplay.Container.exe' You can then see how much each process has written, which shouldn't usually be very much at all. I measured my own PC on an older driver version ( 621.01 ) and this process had only written 63 MB in an hour of uptime; if you're on the most recent GeForce driver package (621.24), and NVDisplay.Container.exe has a number of gigabytes next to it (it's in bytes, so get your calculator out), you've been bit by the bug. The affected d…

title: Don't stress about collectathon completionism in Queen's Domain: It eventually gives you tools to help find hidden treasures

body: Queen's Domain has, by my count, four categories of collectible you have to hoover up if you want to see its more hidden endings, and some of them are real bastards to find⁠—I'd resigned myself to queueing up guides on YouTube to get it all done. Guides are great, you might still need them for some of the collectibles, and if there's one game that feels like it was designed with Google/Reddit/forum help in mind, it's Queen's Domain. But I was thrilled to discover that, very late in the game, Queen's Domain provides a waypoint tool to guide you to its hidden collectibles. It turned what I worried would be a tedious process into yet another example of this game's boundless capacity for surprise and discovery. I know I would have appreciated the heads-up, the permission to not worry about finding them all earlier in my playtime. If that's how you felt, and you aren't looking for spoilers, great: You can stop reading here. Granted, the spoilers in Queen's Domain are so absurd and out there as to be incomprehensible to someone early on in a playthrough. title: GTA 5's Steam concurrents have gone up rather than down now that GTA 6 is out, suggesting a lot of PC players are waiting
summary: We have GTA 6 at home.
body: Pour one out for the PC gamers who are now forced to watch everyone frolic in the streets of Grand Theft Auto 6 on consoles this week. The next best thing on PC is GTA 5, and its recent Steam concurrents suggest people are trying their best to fight the FOMO until Rockstar decides to bring the new one over. You might assume GTA 5 player counts would tank now that it's old news, but the numbers have actually jumped up a bit in the last month. SteamDB shows a peak of around 87,000 concurrent players in the last day, an almost 10% increase from October. There's been a bit of a dip today—which could partially be attributed to GTA 6 finally becoming available in every region—but it's not as sharp of a drop as you'd think it'd be for a 13-year-old game. In fact, GTA 5 has steadily kept a good amount of players over the last year, with major spikes happening around the occasional price discount. It usually hovers around 40,000 to 50,000 average concurrent players, and GTA 6's release hasn't broken the pattern. That's the beauty of PC gaming for you: Steam sales and mods keep games like this chugging along years after they'd be considered cutting edge. (Image credit: SteamDB) GTA 5 holdou…

summary: The 2TB model will be "especially constrained": Valve has closed the waitlist and says it doesn't know how many it will be able to make, or at what price they'll be sold.
body: Valve has good news and bad news for anyone interested in buying a Steam Machine. All current reservations for the 512GB model have been fulfilled and there's stock remaining, so if you want one you can just head over to the purchase page and buy it—but the 2TB model is in shorter supply so signups for the waitlist are no longer being taken. And, sorry to say, there's also worse news: Valve says it won't be able to produce them in the quantities it had planned, and the price could increase. Despite their high prices, demand for Steam Machines was high enough that Valve implemented a randomized lottery system to buy one: Prospective purchasers signed up for a shot, a randomized selection were put in a reservation queue with a Steam Machine reserved in their name, and everyone else went to the waiting list to be notified when more reservation spots came open. Valve said in July that it expected to have the reservation queue caught up by the end of 2026 , and that's now the case with the 512GB model: They're in an "an add-to-cart status," meaning that while supplies last, you can purchase one and it will be shipped straight away. title: If you bounced off indie hit Queen's Domain, try using the cheat code book to give yourself a gun
summary: Would somebody please get this man a gun.
body: Queen's Domain's melee combat isn't for everyone: Luckily there's an in-game cheat book you can use to get a gun (and it doesn't bork your achievements cheevos or nothin'). First person King's Field/Metroid Prime-like Queen's Domain has quickly become a top-two shortlister for my personal game of the year , but it can be a prickly, difficult-to-recommend game, particularly in its first 30 minutes or so before you get the game-defining Endu airdash sword. I'm of a mind with news writer Josh Wolens that the contrast between pre- and post-Endu gameplay really helps sell the game's power curve, but our coworkers Andy Chalk and Morgan Park both bounced off Queen's Domain's admittedly sluggish melee combat. There isn't a difficulty selection in Queen's Domain, but there is something close to it: A "witch's grimoire" where you can input codes to receive unique items. Most of these are references to streamers, content creators, or other indie developers. While referential, they mesh surprisingly well with Queen's Domain's aesthetic, and I don't think they threaten its overall very deliberate sense of progression. body: I've been playing GTA 6 through the morning to try to see what the fuss is about, and now I totally get it. After mere hours in the game, I'm already coming to terms with the scale of it; not just the size of the map, but the attention to detail on every object and interaction. But I have to remind myself, this is sure to be the worst version of GTA 6 we'll ever play. That sounds like an insult, but I mean the exact opposite. If this is where the game is at launch, at its most barebones, running on years-old consoles on their way out, then think of what it will be like at its peak. body: Corsair is continuing the 2026 trend of brands pushing out new and innovative mouse technologies . In this case, it's all in the 'PureVector' part of the name. In practice, I've found that PureVector hasn't improved my aim, both subjectively while gaming and objectively based on multiple AimLabs tests. Some pro players that Corsair highlights claim it's helped them, so your mileage may vary. Apart from PureVector, though, the mouse itself deserves some attention, as it's still a very performant, lightweight mouse for competitive gaming. It has some upgrades compared to its predecessor, the Sabre V2 Pro , too. Buy if… ✅ You want to try the latest tech: You might get better results than I did with PureVector.
